Eigen3 linear algebra backend
nodes.rationale: All Chrono dense and sparse matrices are aliases of Eigen types with row-major storage; ChVector3/ChVector2 are deliberately NOT Eigen types.

nodes.label: ChMatrixNM fixed-size matrix
nodes.rationale: Fixed sizes pay off below roughly 16 elements per dimension because Eigen avoids heap allocation and unrolls loops; very large fixed matrices risk stack overflow.

nodes.label: ChMatrix33 (3x3 fixed)
nodes.rationale: Specialized for rotation matrices and 3D inertia tensors, with dedicated coordinate/rotation constructors.

nodes.label: ChFunction y=f(x) objects
nodes.rationale: Scalar function objects used wherever a prescribed motion or signal is needed; the base class supplies numerical derivatives, which a subclass can override with analytic ones for higher precision.

nodes.label: ChQuadrature (Gauss-Legendre)
nodes.rationale: Exact when the integrand is a polynomial of degree <= the quadrature order; coefficients are precomputed for N<10 because typical use is order 1..10.

nodes.label: ChIntegrable1D / ChIntegrable2D interfaces

Modal analysis
nodes.rationale: Extracts mode shapes, frequencies and damping ratios of structures and mechanisms; supports finite elements, rigid bodies, constraints and rigid-body modes so a whole mechanism (not only an FE mesh) can be characterized.

nodes.label: Modal reduction
nodes.rationale: Trades model fidelity for speed: replaces internal states with a reduced basis that preserves behavior over a chosen frequency band, giving fewer states and a large performance gain while the full internal state is still reconstructed for visualization. Limitation accepted by design: only linear dynamics of the subassembly is supported, so the subassembly cannot undergo large rotations (e.g. a helicopter blade).

nodes.label: Eigenvalue solvers (pure-matrix layer)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately decoupled from ChSystem/ChAssembly so they operate on pure matrices only; accept real matrices, implement shift-and-invert iterative methods, handle sparse matrices, and return the lowest eigenvalues relative to the shift. Not intended for direct use by the average user.

nodes.label: Modal solvers (ChAssembly interface layer)
nodes.rationale: Interface classes that run an eigenvalue solver on a ChAssembly and can include damping; the preferred entry point for the average user. Split undamped vs damped because the damped problem is always unsymmetric and therefore requires an unsymmetric eigenvalue solver.

nodes.label: ChModalAssembly
nodes.rationale: Splits its contents into boundary items (Add(), on the border with the external world) and internal items (AddInternal(), later reduced), so DoModalReduction() knows which DOFs must be retained for coupling and which may be condensed away.

nodes.label: ChModalVisualSystemIrrlicht
nodes.rationale: Header-only and therefore not shipped in a shared library; CMake enables it automatically when the Irrlicht module is on, since mode-shape visualization requires Irrlicht. Templated on double or std::complex<double> to match the eigenvalue solver in use, and AttachAssembly must be called only after Solve().

nodes.label: ChAssembly (top-level system assembly)
nodes.rationale: ChSystem holds one top-level ChAssembly which may nest further assemblies, so only a subset of the system can be analyzed or reduced by adding objects to a sub-assembly and the sub-assembly to the system.

nodes.label: Three-file YAML specification hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Model, solver and simulation concerns are split into three files (top-level simulation file plus a model file and a solver file) so models and solver settings can be reused independently. FSI deepens the hierarchy because a coupled problem must reference both an MBS simulation file and a fluid simulation file.

nodes.label: Model reference frame (M)
nodes.rationale: All body poses, joint frames and TSDA endpoints are given relative to an implied model frame rather than the global frame; the caller supplies the global-to-model transform at instantiation so the same YAML model can be placed multiple times in one scene at different locations and orientations.

nodes.label: Body reference frame vs centroidal frame
nodes.rationale: Bodies are specified in the most general and flexible way: an arbitrary body reference frame B, with the centroidal frame C given as a transform from B, inertia expressed in C, and all collision/visualization geometry expressed in B.

nodes.label: run_chrono runner application
nodes.rationale: Single executable that runs any simulation fully described by YAML; --no_output and --no_visualization override the YAML settings so a scripted or headless run needs no file edits. The output directory is created if missing but its parents must already exist.

nodes.label: FSI simulation YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Top-level co-simulation file: references an MBS simulation file and a fluid simulation file by relative path, describes the coupling, and owns the co-simulation metastep, so any fluid solver implementing the Chrono::FSI API can be plugged in.

nodes.label: fsi_bodies coupling specification
nodes.rationale: Names MBS bodies that interact with the fluid plus the shapes used to generate fluid-solid interface markers. Lookup is by name and matches every instance of that body, so one entry covers a multiply-instantiated MBS model; an unmatched name is a warning, not an error, so partial models still run.

nodes.label: Co-simulation metastep
nodes.rationale: A separate outer time_step at which the MBS and fluid solvers exchange data, distinct from each solver's own internal integration step.

nodes.label: data_path relocatable file resolution
nodes.rationale: Shared ABSOLUTE/RELATIVE + root convention used across every Chrono YAML schema so a specification directory can be moved without rewriting every referenced data file path; defaults to absolute paths.

nodes.label: FSI output options (format/mode/fps)
nodes.rationale: format is mandatory whenever the output key is present, and HDF5 silently degrades to NONE in a build without HDF5 support so the same YAML runs on any build.

nodes.label: FSI run-time visualization options
nodes.rationale: Presence of the key alone enables rendering (no type entry at this level). Camera and general rendering settings live here, while body shapes come from the referenced MBS file and fluid-phase rendering from the referenced fluid file - one place per concern.

nodes.label: physics_problem: CFD vs CRM
nodes.rationale: One SPH machinery serves two physics: incompressible fluid (CFD, parameterized by fluid_properties) and homogenized granular dynamics (CRM, parameterized by soil_properties with a mu(I) friction law), so the choice of property block follows from this single enum.

nodes.label: fluid_domain and container
nodes.rationale: Same property set for the initially filled region and the confining container, shaped by geometry_type (CARTESIAN box vs CYLINDRICAL annulus). Walls may be declared on the fluid domain OR on a container but not both - declaring a container after fluid_domain already declared walls is an error, which keeps a single unambiguous owner of the boundary.

nodes.label: computational_domain and BC types
nodes.rationale: AABB bounding the region in which particles are tracked, with per-direction NONE/PERIODIC/INLET_OUTLET boundary conditions. For CARTESIAN geometry a non-NONE BC requires that no fluid-domain wall was defined normal to that direction, since a solid wall and a periodic/inlet-outlet boundary in the same direction would conflict.

nodes.label: wave_tank shorthand
nodes.rationale: Self-contained alternative to explicit domain definitions: when present, fluid_domain, container and computational_domain are all ignored. Restricted to physics_problem CFD and CARTESIAN geometry, and drives a PISTON or FLAP wave maker through a generic time function with an optional delay.

nodes.label: SPH initial_states (depth-based pressure)
nodes.rationale: Initializes particle pressure hydrostatically from depth relative to zero_height, which suppresses the startup transient a zero-pressure initialization would produce.

nodes.label: FSI-SPH simulation YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Binds an SPH model file to an SPH solver file and owns fluid-phase output and visualization; camera and general rendering deliberately belong to the parent FSI simulation file instead.

nodes.label: SPH particle color_map
nodes.rationale: Colors particles by HEIGHT/VELOCITY/DENSITY/PRESSURE over an explicit min-max range; up applies only to HEIGHT and bimodal is required for PRESSURE because pressure is naturally two-sided about zero.

nodes.label: Half-space marker visibility
nodes.rationale: Hides markers by testing their position against a set of planes with ALL or ANY combination, giving cut-away views into a dense particle field without changing the simulation.

nodes.label: splashsurf fluid surface reconstruction
nodes.rationale: Marching-cubes iso-surface over the particle field; smoothing_length and cube_size are expressed in multiples of the particle radius and surface_threshold in multiples of rest density, so defaults stay resolution-independent.

nodes.label: FSI-SPH solver YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Every object is optional and any omitted property keeps its default, so a minimal solver file is valid. The file carries no output or visualization settings; those belong to the FSI-SPH simulation file.

nodes.label: Weakly compressible SPH method parameters
nodes.rationale: Base weakly compressible formulation: ISOTHERMAL or TAIT equation of state, delta-SPH density diffusion on by default to damp density noise, a max_velocity used for scaling, and a CRM-only free_surface_threshold compared against the divergence of the position field to flag free-surface particles.

nodes.label: SPH kernel and resolution
nodes.rationale: Kernel length is defined as d0_multiplier * initial_spacing, so changing particle resolution rescales the smoothing length automatically.

nodes.label: Consistent (corrected) SPH discretization
nodes.rationale: Optional G-matrix gradient and L-matrix Laplacian corrections, off by default because they cost more than the uncorrected operators.

nodes.label: SPH integration scheme and time step
nodes.rationale: EULER/RK2/VERLET/SYMPLECTIC/IMPLICIT_SPH; time_step is mandatory whenever the integration object exists since there is no safe default fluid step.

nodes.label: Proximity (neighbor) search cadence
nodes.rationale: num_proximity_search_steps trades neighbor-list accuracy against rebuild cost; defaults to rebuilding every step.

nodes.label: Particle shifting algorithms
nodes.rationale: NONE/PPST/XSPH/PPST_XSPH/DIFFUSION/DIFFUSION_XSPH keep particle distributions regular; which coefficients matter depends on the selected method, and shifting_beta_implicit applies only under the IMPLICIT_SPH scheme.

nodes.label: Viscosity treatment
nodes.rationale: LAMINAR uses the physical viscosity from the SPH model file's fluid_properties, while the ARTIFICIAL_* methods use the artificial_viscosity coefficient instead - so the model file and solver file are coupled through this choice.

nodes.label: Linear time-domain potential-flow hydrodynamics
nodes.rationale: TDPF does not discretize the fluid at all: it applies added mass, radiation damping and wave excitation forces to the FSI bodies from pre-computed frequency-domain coefficients read from an HDF5 file, which is why it needs no fluid solver settings.

nodes.label: TDPF wave conditions
nodes.rationale: NONE/REGULAR/IRREGULAR; IRREGULAR is accepted by the parser but not yet implemented and silently generates no waves.

nodes.label: TDPF wave-mesh visualization
nodes.rationale: Renders the water surface as a mesh refreshed at update_fps and optionally colored by HEIGHT or VELOCITY; camera and general rendering come from the parent FSI simulation file.

nodes.label: FSI-TDPF solver YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Contains only the chrono-version key: TDPF represents applied forces on FSI bodies rather than an independent fluid integration, so it uses the MBS solver and needs no integrator or solver settings of its own. The file exists only to keep the uniform simulation/model/solver triple.

nodes.label: MBS model YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Lists all physics items of a mechanical system: bodies (required), joints, passive force elements, motors and actuators, constraints and external loads. Enum values are accepted in any case (point_line, POINT_LINE, PoInT_LiNe) to keep hand-written YAML forgiving.

nodes.label: YAML body specification
nodes.rationale: Mass and inertia moments are required only if the body is not fixed; orientation accepts either Euler-Cardan angles [yaw, pitch, roll] or a quaternion [e0..e3]; inertia is expressed in the centroidal frame while geometry is expressed in the body reference frame.

nodes.label: Contact materials and collision shapes
nodes.rationale: Materials and shapes are separate lists joined by material name, so more shapes than materials can share one material. The same friction/restitution values behave differently under SMC and NSC; under SMC the user may give either material physical properties (Young modulus, Poisson ratio) or spring-damper coefficients (normal/tangential stiffness and damping).

nodes.label: Body visualization shapes vs model_file
nodes.rationale: A model_file is passed as-is to the run-time visualization system, whereas a MESH shape is assumed to be an OBJ Wavefront file and therefore also supports translation, rotation and scaling.

nodes.label: Joints (kinematic or bushing)
nodes.rationale: One joint entry becomes an ideal kinematic constraint, or a stiff-compliance bushing if bushing_data is present, so stiffness can be introduced without restructuring the model. Bushings are prohibited for PRISMATIC, CYLINDRICAL, POINT_LINE and POINT_PLANE joints.

nodes.label: bushing_data compliance
nodes.rationale: Top-level stiffness/damping relax the constrained DOFs of the ideal joint; the nested DOF object optionally adds compliance along the unconstrained DOF, which defaults to 0.0 when the DOF object is absent.

nodes.label: TSDA translational spring-damper
nodes.rationale: One element type covers three regimes selected purely by which keys are present: linear (spring_coefficient/damping_coefficient), degressive damper (damping_coefficient plus degressivity_compression and degressivity_expansion, and no spring_coefficient), and nonlinear tabular data (spring_curve_data, damping_curve_data, or deformation/map_data) linearly interpolated at run time.

nodes.label: RSDA rotational spring-damper
nodes.rationale: Applies torques about an axis with a free_angle and preload; linear and nonlinear torques are specified exactly like the corresponding TSDA forces.

nodes.label: Motors (LINEAR / ROTATION)
nodes.rationale: Actuation is expressed at the POSITION, SPEED or FORCE level through a time function, and the accompanying kinematic guide (FREE/PRISMATIC/SPHERICAL) or spindle (FREE/REVOLUTE/CYLINDRICAL) constraint is chosen separately, so actuation and constraint concerns stay independent.

nodes.label: Generic time-function object
nodes.rationale: Only type is required and it selects which further fields are valid: CONSTANT, POLYNOMIAL, SINE, RAMP, DATA (linearly interpolated points), and CONTROLLER which defers the value to an external controller. Every type except CONTROLLER accepts an optional repeat block (start/width/shift) to replicate the function periodically.

nodes.label: Body loads and load controllers
nodes.rationale: FORCE or TORQUE applied to a named body, with explicit local_load and local_point flags so the frame of the load vector and its application point are never implicit.

nodes.label: FEA components in the MBS model
nodes.rationale: Requires the Chrono::FEA module; in a build without it the whole FEA object is ignored with a warning rather than failing. Support is explicitly partial: of the beam section types only ANCF_CABLE is implemented, no FEA material type is implemented, shells are not implemented, and only NODE_FRAME, NODESLOPE_FRAME and NODE_NODE constraints exist - an unimplemented type raises a run-time error. Note the misspelled Rayleight_damping key.

nodes.label: FEA constraints and node references
nodes.rationale: A node is addressed by mesh name plus a 1-based index within that mesh, where a beam's name doubles as its mesh name. NODE_FRAME ties a node to a body, NODESLOPE_FRAME additionally constrains the node slope direction, NODE_NODE ties two FEA nodes.

MBS simulation YAML schema
nodes.rationale: type must be MBS; binds a model file and a solver file by relative path and adds optional simulation, output and visualization blocks.

nodes.label: num_threads (chrono/collision/eigen/pardiso)
nodes.rationale: Thread counts are set per parallel component rather than globally, because Chrono, collision detection, Eigen and PARDISO scale differently; the pardiso entry is honored only when the solver file selects the PARDISO solver type.

nodes.label: MBS visualization type gate
nodes.rationale: Rendering is enabled only when the visualization key exists AND its type is other than NONE, so omitting the key and writing type: NONE are deliberately equivalent.

nodes.label: enforce_realtime and end_time
nodes.rationale: end_time defaults to -1 meaning an infinite simulation.

nodes.label: MBS solver YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Only contact_method is required; omitting integrator yields EULER_IMPLICIT_LINEARIZED with a 1e-3 step and omitting solver yields BARZILAI_BORWEIN with defaults. Carries no output or visualization settings - those belong to the MBS simulation file.

nodes.label: Time integrator types
nodes.rationale: EULER_IMPLICIT_LINEARIZED / EULER_IMPLICIT_PROJECTED / EULER_IMPLICIT / HHT; both type and time_step are required whenever the integrator object is present. Tolerances are split into state and Lagrange-multiplier absolute tolerances because multipliers live on a different scale (default 1e2 vs 1e-4).

nodes.label: DVI and linear solver types
nodes.rationale: Three families with distinct parameter sets: iterative DVI (BARZILAI_BORWEIN, APGD, PSOR) with overrelaxation and sharpness factors, iterative Krylov linear (BICGSTAB, MINRES, GMRES) with a residual tolerance, and direct sparse (SPARSE_LU, SPARSE_QR, PARDISO, MUMPS) with sparsity-pattern locking and a pattern learner available only for SPARSE_LU/SPARSE_QR. PARDISO and MUMPS require the corresponding optional Chrono module.

nodes.label: Vehicle model YAML schema
nodes.rationale: Rather than re-describing sub-systems in YAML, the vehicle model file only points at existing Chrono::Vehicle JSON specification files. Only model is a nested object; terrain_json, initial_position, initial_yaw and chase_camera sit at the top level as siblings of model.

nodes.label: Vehicle JSON sub-system references
nodes.rationale: vehicle_json, engine_json and transmission_json are required and tire_json is required only for wheeled vehicles. The wheeled/tracked distinction is never stated in the YAML: it is inferred from the Template field of the vehicle JSON file, so one YAML shape serves both.

nodes.label: chase_camera settings
nodes.rationale: All-or-nothing block: if chase_camera is present then chassis_point, chase_distance and chase_height are all required.

nodes.label: initial_yaw degree convention
nodes.rationale: initial_yaw is always interpreted in degrees, deliberately independent of the model's angle_degrees setting.

nodes.label: Vehicle simulation YAML schema
nodes.rationale: type must be VEHICLE; pairs a vehicle model file with an MBS solver file, reusing the MBS solver schema unchanged rather than defining a vehicle-specific one.

nodes.label: Fixed vehicle sub-system visualization types
nodes.rationale: The visualization type key controls only plain rigid bodies; the visualization types used for chassis, suspension, steering, wheels, tires and tracked-vehicle components are currently fixed by the parser and cannot be set from YAML.

nodes.label: ChPythonEngine
nodes.rationale: Runs generic Python code from C++ and exchanges data through variables. Explicitly NOT PyChrono: ChPythonEngine drives Python from C++, whereas PyChrono is a stand-alone Python library wrapping Chrono C++.

nodes.label: ChPythonEngine::ImportSolidWorksSystem()
nodes.rationale: Imports SolidWorks models exported to Python; documented as not the only route for importing SolidWorks models.

nodes.label: ChMeshFileLoader
nodes.rationale: Lives in the main Chrono module rather than PARSERS so FE mesh import (Abaqus, TetGen, GMF/LS-DYNA, OBJ) needs no optional module; deliberately limited to very specific elements and not a full-fledged FE import tool.

nodes.label: URDF model import
nodes.rationale: Requires an external library, which is why it is an optional capability of the Parsers module.

nodes.label: Chrono YAML parser classes
nodes.rationale: Cache model information and simulation settings from YAML input, then populate a Chrono, Chrono::Vehicle or Chrono::FSI system and set solver and simulation parameters, so a full simulation needs no user C++ code.

nodes.label: PyChrono conda package install
nodes.rationale: Recommended route: precompiled modules for Linux, Windows and macOS and several Python 3 versions, installed in one step into a dedicated conda environment. Packages built from a release carry the 'release' label and those from the development branch the 'main' label. Caveat: cascade, vsg3d and ROS modules are not yet in the conda build.

nodes.label: Building PyChrono from the C++ API
nodes.rationale: More complicated but the only way to get the most up-to-date PyChrono and the modules missing from conda. Requires Python 3.2 or greater, and PYTHONPATH must be extended with the bin/ directory of the Chrono build tree.

nodes.label: AMD GPU / ROCm PyChrono workflow
nodes.rationale: CPU PyChrono can be built without the NVIDIA CUDA toolkit alongside a PyTorch ROCm stack on AMD Instinct or Radeon GPUs; docs/README_AMD_GPU.md covers the CPU vs HIP/FSI workflows, Eigen3 and SWIG prerequisites, and ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES on multi-GPU hosts.

nodes.label: PyChrono
nodes.rationale: A Python module giving access to a large part of the Chrono API without any C++ programming. Traded off deliberately: Python is simple, interpretable on the fly, has a rich third-party ecosystem (Matplotlib, NumPy) and needs a minimal install, but is slower than C++ and the Python module does not cover all C++ API features.

nodes.label: PyChrono linear algebra / NumPy interoperability
nodes.rationale: ChMatrixDynamicd and ChVectorDynamicd are interfaced with plain Python lists (SetMatr/GetMatr), which lets any third-party package such as NumPy do the linear algebra without a dedicated binding layer.

nodes.label: Operator overloading in PyChrono vectors and quaternions
nodes.rationale: Most C++ operator overloads carry over (~ conjugate, ^ dot product, % quaternion product), so C++ example code translates almost literally.

nodes.label: No generated Python API documentation
nodes.rationale: There is no Sphinx automated generation of Python API docs; because most classes behave like their C++ counterparts, users are directed to the C++ API documentation and to IDE code completion instead.

nodes.label: SWIG wrapping layer
nodes.rationale: PyChrono is a set of Python modules mirroring Chrono units, generated through SWIG; SWIG's limitations (no nested classes, no templates) directly shape the Python API surface.

nodes.label: Templated classes wrapped as named specializations
nodes.rationale: Python has no template support, so each relevant C++ specialization is wrapped under its C++ alias name (ChVector3d, ChQuaterniond, ChMatrixDynamicd, ChFramed...). std::vector containers get a vector_ prefix, e.g. chrono.vector_ChVector3d for std::vector<ChVector<double>>.

nodes.label: Python object creation and assignment semantics
nodes.rationale: There is only one creation form in Python and lifetime is managed automatically, removing the C++ stack-vs-heap choice and the matching delete. The = operator assigns another handle rather than copying, so two names can refer to one ChSystem.

nodes.label: Shared pointers handled automatically
nodes.rationale: Chrono's C++ shared pointers are template-based and templates are unsupported in Python, but this is not an issue because PyChrono handles shared-pointer objects automatically: constructing the Python object also creates the referenced object, and further handles are made by plain assignment.

nodes.label: ChVector x/y/z as members instead of accessor calls
nodes.rationale: The C++ x()/y()/z() reference-returning accessors are mapped to direct member access in Python to avoid issues with returning references; the same applies to quaternion components e0..e3.

nodes.label: Upcasting vs manual downcasting (CastToXXX)
nodes.rationale: Upcasting of derived to base works automatically, including for shared pointers. Downcasting is the hard direction: it is automatic only for classes derived from ChFunction and ChAsset, otherwise the user calls a CastToXXX() helper, the Python analogue of dynamic_cast<derived>(base).

nodes.label: Nested class flattening
nodes.rationale: SWIG does not support nested classes in Python, so instead of ignoring them PyChrono flattens every nested Chrono class into the upper namespace level; nested enum classes become underscore-joined names such as VisualizationType_MESH.

nodes.label: Detecting unmapped C++ classes
nodes.rationale: A correctly wrapped return value echoes as a pychrono type proxying a Swig Object; an unmapped one echoes only as a bare Swig Object pointer and is unusable from Python. This gives users a concrete test for coverage gaps to report.

nodes.label: ChROSHandler
nodes.rationale: A handler owns the publishers and subscriptions for exactly one feature (a sensor, a body's state, a control input) and is called at a fixed rate. Adding a ROS pathway means subclassing ChROSHandler and registering an instance with ChROSManager - a single extension point instead of per-feature plumbing.

nodes.label: ChROSManager
nodes.rationale: Update() ticks each registered handler at its own rate and drains incoming subscriptions, returning false when the node has stopped so the simulation loop can break.

nodes.label: ChROSBridge
nodes.rationale: Handed to Initialize(); creates publishers and subscriptions by topic plus type-name string, serializes and deserializes the message, and exposes DescribeType() for field discovery.

nodes.label: ChROSPublisher
nodes.rationale: NewMessage()/Publish() pair, plus GetSubscriptionCount() so a handler can skip expensive extraction while nobody is subscribed.

nodes.label: ChROSMessageView
nodes.rationale: Read-side counterpart of the message builder: GetDouble/GetInt/GetString by dotted path, plus GetCount(path) and GetMessage(path, i) for sequences.

nodes.label: Set/get message fields by dotted path
nodes.rationale: Because message types are resolved at run time from the sourced ROS environment, fields are addressed by name (e.g. "header.frame_id") through typed setters SetBool/SetInt/SetUInt/SetDouble/SetString/SetStringArray, with SetTime for builtin_interfaces/Time and AppendMessage(path) for sequences of nested messages. Unset fields serialize as zero/empty.

nodes.label: Blob API for bulk primitive arrays
nodes.rationale: Camera pixels, lidar points and any T[] bypass the per-field setters and copy the buffer once. SetBlob does not copy - the source buffer must stay alive until Publish() returns within the same Tick() - while SetBlobCopy is the safe variant. In Python any C-contiguous buffer works, and GetMemoryView is zero-copy but valid only inside the callback.

nodes.label: Single-threaded handler execution model
nodes.rationale: Subscription callbacks run inside ChROSManager::Update() on the simulation thread, the same thread as Tick(), so reading or writing Chrono objects from a callback needs no locking. The corollary is a prohibition: do not spawn threads that touch Chrono objects or call into a handler.

nodes.label: Handler rate measured in simulation time
nodes.rationale: The constructor rate is in simulation time so a handler ticks consistently no matter how fast the simulation runs relative to real time; 0 means every step. Wall-clock pacing is left to the application via ChRealtimeStepTimer, and header.stamp fields plus a registered ChROSClockHandler let downstream nodes run with use_sim_time:=true.

nodes.label: Custom message packages without registration
nodes.rationale: Any message type whose package is built and sourced in the environment is usable by name with no registration step; if the package is missing, Initialize() fails with an error naming it rather than failing later at publish time.

nodes.label: ChROSQoS presets
nodes.rationale: Optional argument to CreatePublisher/CreateSubscription. Named presets Default(), SensorData(), Clock() and Latched() cover the common cases - Latched is transient-local, needed for latched topics such as /robot_description - with explicit reliability, durability and history depth available underneath.

nodes.label: Custom handlers in Python
nodes.rationale: pychrono.ros mirrors the C++ handler contract (subclass chros.ChROSHandler, implement Initialize/Tick) but replaces typed setters with item syntax msg["field"] = value, and subscribers subclass chros.ChROSSubscriptionCallback with OnMessage(view).

nodes.label: ChROSDriverInputsHandler
nodes.rationale: Reference example of a subscriber handler using a custom message package (chrono_ros_interfaces/msg/DriverInputs).

nodes.label: Chrono::ROS internal IPC protocol
nodes.rationale: Documented not because users need it - handlers and the message API hide it entirely - but for debugging the bridge, porting to a new ROS 2 distribution, or understanding how messages cross the process boundary.

nodes.label: chrono_ros_node subprocess
nodes.rationale: Strict symbol separation: the simulation process contains no ROS symbols and the subprocess contains no Chrono physics symbols, joined by a bidirectional shared-memory channel. The subprocess uses rclcpp generic publishers/subscriptions with introspection type support so it never needs compiled message types.

nodes.label: IPC frame kinds
nodes.rationale: Fixed frame set (HELLO, DESCRIBE_TYPE, TYPE_SCHEMA, VALIDATE_TYPE, VALIDATE_RESULT, ADVERTISE, ADVERTISE_ACK, PUBLISH, RECEIVED, UNADVERTISE, CHANNEL_INFO, SHUTDOWN), each a header of magic, protocol version, kind, channel_id, sim_time_ns and payload_size followed by its payload.

nodes.label: CHANNEL_INFO subscriber counting
nodes.rationale: Carries live subscriber/publisher counts updated as the ROS graph changes; this is the mechanism behind ChROSPublisher::GetSubscriptionCount() and therefore behind a handler skipping work when nobody is listening.

nodes.label: Runtime type schema blob
nodes.rationale: The simulation process never parses .msg files. On first use of a type it sends DESCRIBE_TYPE; the subprocess resolves the name through the sourced ROS environment, walks rosidl introspection type support recursively, and returns a packed schema blob from which the bridge builds its serializer and deserializer - which is why any installed message type, custom packages included, works by name with no code in Chrono. The blob stays a simple versioned packed little-endian format because both ends are built from the same source tree and it never crosses a version boundary.

nodes.label: XCDR1 plain-CDR encoding
nodes.rationale: The payload crossing the channel is the ROS message serialized as CDR - the same bytes ROS 2 puts on the wire - encoded by a small dependency-free codec in the simulation process. XCDR1 is sufficient because all ROS 2 message types are @final and are serialized as plain CDR by both rmw_fastrtps and rmw_cyclonedds.

nodes.label: Per-type run-time codec validation
nodes.rationale: The codec is verified per type at run time rather than trusted by assertion: at Initialize() the bridge sends a canonical test-pattern message via VALIDATE_TYPE, the subprocess round-trips it through rclcpp serialization and byte-compares, so a mismatch (e.g. a future rmw switching to XCDR2) aborts Initialize() with a precise error instead of publishing corrupt data. Implementation note: rmw serializers do not guarantee interior padding bytes, so the node zero-fills its re-serialization buffer to keep skipped padding from being reported as field mismatches.

nodes.label: Schema-driven bridge (Chrono 10.0 change)
nodes.rationale: A message type is now identified by its ROS type-name string and serialized to/from CDR by Chrono itself over shared memory, so the ROS subprocess is generic and no longer compiled per message type. Built-in handlers keep their interfaces, but a custom handler written against the old design must be rewritten - the payoff is no IPC struct, no message-type enum, no subprocess file and no Chrono rebuild, plus custom handlers in Python.

nodes.label: ROS node process separation (Chrono 9.0 change)
nodes.rationale: The ROS 2 node was moved into a separate process connected over shared memory specifically to resolve and prevent symbol collisions between the ROS 2 and Chrono process spaces; the schema-driven bridge retains this separation.

nodes.label: Chrono::ROS module
nodes.rationale: Developed by SBEL at UW-Madison to provide a simple, extensible interface between Chrono and ROS 2 so Chrono can be dropped directly into ROS autonomy-stack development; built on ROS 2's existing network capabilities and reusing existing ROS concepts (publishers, subscribers, topics) rather than inventing new ones.

nodes.label: Handler coverage across Chrono modules
nodes.rationale: Chrono::ROS is not tied to any one Chrono module; general-purpose handlers exist for Chrono::Vehicle and Chrono::Sensor for rapid prototyping, and anything else is reached by writing a custom handler. The PyChrono/Chrono::Python wrapper is supported.

nodes.label: Time Synchronization and Sim-to-Real Best Practices
ChROSClockHandler
nodes.rationale: Publishes simulation time on /clock so the simulation, not the wall clock, is the master clock for the whole ROS graph.

nodes.label: use_sim_time parameter
nodes.rationale: Set true in simulation and false on hardware so the same node code runs in both; a node with use_sim_time true and no /clock publisher blocks forever waiting for time.

nodes.label: Fixed timestep and real-time factor
nodes.rationale: Simulation time is decoupled from wall time: the loop runs as fast as it can or is throttled to real time with ChRealtimeStepTimer. This matches the standard physics/robotics convention (Gazebo max-step-size and real-time-factor).

nodes.label: ROS-clock timer vs create_wall_timer
nodes.rationale: create_wall_timer always uses the steady clock and ignores use_sim_time, so a control loop built on it runs at wall-clock rate regardless of simulation time - the most common source of sim/real timing mismatch.

nodes.label: Behavioral vs bit reproducibility
nodes.rationale: The simulation does not block on ROS, so OS scheduling and transport jitter shift command arrival by a step or two. Behavioral reproducibility is enough for tuning, validation and HIL; bit-exactness requires lock-step gating or running control in-process as a C++ ChROSHandler.

nodes.label: Lock-step (synchronous) stepping
nodes.rationale: Gating each step on the controller reply makes the closed loop bit-reproducible, but freezes the world while the controller computes so real compute latency is hidden - good for training and regression, wrong for latency-sensitive sim-to-real validation.

nodes.label: Compute latency and causality
nodes.rationale: On hardware, control and CV inference consume wall time while the world moves. Real-time-paced simulation reproduces that causally; lock-stepping is deterministic but optimistic.

nodes.label: Multiple simulations in one ROS graph
nodes.rationale: Only one participant may publish /clock; followers subscribe and advance DoStepDynamics only up to the received time. This coordinates time only - for large-scale distributed multi-agent co-simulation SynChrono is the purpose-built tool.

nodes.label: Shared /tf with unique frame ids
nodes.rationale: /tf is multi-publisher by convention and tf2 aggregates by frame pair, so namespaced frame ids (robot1/base_link) keep trees from colliding.

nodes.label: ChGPSSensor
nodes.rationale: Computes latitude, longitude and altitude from a spherical coordinate system plus a GPS reference location marking the simulation origin; assumes a Z-up, X-East, Y-North Chrono system.

nodes.label: ChNoiseNormalDrift
nodes.rationale: Adds bias drift and a drift time constant on top of Gaussian noise, modelling the slow bias wander characteristic of inertial sensors that a pure normal noise model cannot represent.

nodes.label: IMU as Three Composed Sensors
nodes.rationale: Chrono::Sensor has no monolithic IMU class; accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer are separate sensors used collectively, each with its own update rate, noise model and access filter. Synchronizing their buffers is left to the user, who gates on LaunchedCount to avoid re-reading the same sample.

nodes.label: ChCameraSensor
nodes.rationale: Synthetic images are generated with GPU ray tracing through NVIDIA OptiX headless rendering, using a physically based BRDF shader that recursively spawns shadow, reflection and refraction rays.

nodes.label: ChOptixEngine
nodes.rationale: Camera update frequency is much lower than physics, so the engine spawns a dedicated rendering thread fed by a render queue and never blocks the main dynamics thread.

nodes.label: ChFilterImgAlias
nodes.rationale: Appended automatically when the camera supersample factor exceeds 1; the setup adjusts resolution and downsamples for antialiasing.

nodes.label: Split main/render thread update model
nodes.rationale: Main thread pushes cameras needing update into a render queue and later collects finished data; the render thread waits on the queue. Decouples slow sensor rates from fast physics stepping.

nodes.label: ChLidarSensor
nodes.rationale: Each lidar beam is sampled by a group of rays set by sample radius and divergence angle; returned intensity is based on diffuse reflectance.

nodes.label: Keyframe scan motion blur
nodes.rationale: The whole scan is processed in a single render step, so keyframes let each beam trace the scene at its own time, reproducing motion of both the scene and the lidar across the sweep.

nodes.label: ChRadarSensor
nodes.rationale: Radar is transmitted as a single continuous wave, so scene movement during a scan is negligible compared to lidar and no keyframe/motion-blur treatment is needed; each ray hit carries velocity, intensity, object ID and range.

nodes.label: ChSensorManager
nodes.rationale: Owns the scene and the sensor list; Update() is called each simulation loop iteration alongside DoStepDynamics.

nodes.label: Sensor filter graph
nodes.rationale: Each sensor carries an extensible ordered filter list so users can model sensor-specific artifacts and pick data formats without modifying the sensor class.

nodes.label: Separate sensor data thread
nodes.rationale: Dynamics runs at order 1 kHz while sensors run at 10-100 Hz, so data curation is moved to its own thread rather than stalling the physics loop.

nodes.label: Multi-GPU render threads
nodes.rationale: Multiple render threads each drive a separate GPU for a group of sensors, which matters for multi-agent scenes with many sensors at different update rates.

nodes.label: Reproducible stochastic sensors
nodes.rationale: Per-pixel RNGs default to wall-clock seeding, which is right for simulation but blocks byte-exact comparison; ChSensorManager::SetRandomSeed pins a base seed instead.

nodes.label: ChSensorManager::SetRandomSeed
nodes.rationale: Must be called before AddSensor because the seed is read when a sensor's filters initialize inside AddSensor.

nodes.label: AddSensor registration-order contract
nodes.rationale: Random streams derive from AddSensor order, so adding, removing or reordering sensors changes what other sensors draw even under a fixed seed; comparison runs must build the scene identically.

nodes.label: Per-buffer independent random streams
nodes.rationale: Each buffer derives a distinct cuRAND seed from base seed plus sensor, filter and purpose identity so two cameras, or a camera and a lidar, never draw the same sequence - required for honest sensor-fusion studies.

nodes.label: ChVisualMaterial::Default fallback shading
nodes.rationale: A shape with no ChVisualMaterial renders with the same default Irrlicht and VSG use; values are copied into the device material pool at first sensor update, so mutating the shared default afterwards has no effect.

nodes.label: Sensor ISO reference frame
nodes.rationale: Sensors default to Z-up, X-forward, Y-left to match the vehicle ISO frame, so sensor poses compose directly with Chrono::Vehicle frames.

nodes.label: ChTachometerSensor
nodes.rationale: Unlike the ray-traced sensors, its synthetic data comes from directly querying the parent body's angular velocity about a user-specified axis, so it needs no GPU render pass.

nodes.label: Chrono::SolidWorks add-in
nodes.rationale: Exports SolidWorks assemblies, subassemblies and parts with materials, mates and collision shapes into Chrono; each SubAssembly is one rigid body unless flagged Flexible.

nodes.label: Python / C++ / JSON export targets
nodes.rationale: Python output runs under PyChrono or is parsed in C++ via Chrono::Parsers; C++ output must be compiled with the user project (limiting but useful for testing); JSON output is deserialized through Chrono serialization.

nodes.label: Collision shape specification on export
nodes.rationale: Collision is the most expensive part of a simulation, so only explicitly flagged solid bodies collide. Wrapping complex bodies in primitives is preferred (their material becomes Air); mesh shapes use a sphere sweep whose radius trades robustness against accuracy.

nodes.label: Coordinate-system motor placeholder
nodes.rationale: A top-level Coordinate System plus a custom property acts as the placeholder where a ChLinkMotor is instantiated at export; the property is transparent to SolidWorks installs without the add-in.

nodes.label: How to Add a New Agent to SynChrono
flatc FlatBuffers compiler workflow
nodes.rationale: Only the FlatBuffers header is needed to run SynChrono, but editing schemas requires a built flatc to regenerate SynFlatBuffers_generated.h; FlatBuffers ships as a Chrono submodule so it can be built from source.

nodes.label: Agent.fbs State and Description tables
nodes.rationale: State carries what must be passed every update; Description carries what is needed once for initialization. A new agent must also be added to the union Type.

nodes.label: SynCopterAgent
nodes.rationale: Worked example of deriving from SynAgent: needs a no-argument constructor so it can be built from a description message, plus InitializeZombie, SynchronizeZombie, Update, GatherMessages and GatherDescriptionMessages. Update returns early when the agent is a zombie.

nodes.label: SynMessageFactory
nodes.rationale: Uses dynamic dispatch on the FlatBuffer message_type enum, so every new message type needs another else-if branch - a known extension cost of the factory design.

nodes.label: AgentFactory
nodes.rationale: Uses dynamic_pointer_cast on the incoming description to build a zombie agent from another rank; the description must be fully applied (meshes, propeller count) or the zombie is malformed.

nodes.label: State Synchronization with DDS and MPI
MPI synchronization backend
nodes.rationale: MPI is the SynChrono default because the runtime handles task launch and transport selection (shared memory, InfiniBand, TCP) and is ubiquitous on clusters. Each rank owns one ChSystem.

nodes.label: Two-phase MPI_Allgather / MPI_Allgatherv exchange
nodes.rationale: Vehicles on rigid terrain send fixed-length messages, but deformable terrain does not, so ranks first Allgather message lengths and then run a variable-length Allgatherv to collect the data.

nodes.label: DDS synchronization backend
nodes.rationale: DDS uses Real-Time Publish-Subscribe topics rather than rank-to-rank calls; FastDDS was chosen over RTI Connext to keep with Chrono's open-source philosophy. Preferred outside clusters where MPI is less available and UDP flexibility helps.

nodes.label: SynChronoManager
nodes.rationale: Holds a handle to exactly one SynCommunicator, keeping the SynChrono-level API independent of the transport.

nodes.label: SynDDSPublisher / Subscriber / Topic wrappers
nodes.rationale: Thin wrappers keep SynChrono's DDS usage as minimal as possible - one topic per agent, with data readers and writers handling each agent pair.

nodes.label: SynChrono
nodes.rationale: Developed at SBEL, UW-Madison to extend Chrono physics into the weakly-coupled multi-agent realm: agent dynamics matter individually but not through mutual interaction, so they can be distributed across nodes instead of solved in one monolithic system.

nodes.label: Heartbeat synchronization
nodes.rationale: Nodes step at the same constant timestep but at different real-world speeds; they only rendezvous every heartbeat. Between heartbeats zombie agents stay static, trading spatial fidelity for scalability.

nodes.label: Zombie agent
nodes.rationale: A node's proxy of a remote agent: fixed bodies whose pose is driven entirely by incoming messages. State sent is the minimum needed to reconstruct it - what it looks like (once) and where it is (every heartbeat).

nodes.label: FlatBuffers state serialization
nodes.rationale: Every synchronized agent needs a .fbs schema plus a class that packs and unpacks C++ objects into the wire format.

nodes.label: SynCommunicator
nodes.rationale: Abstracts the transport: MPI and DDS backends exist and others can be added as long as they interchange binary state among all nodes.

nodes.label: SynChrono dependency on Chrono::Vehicle
nodes.rationale: Development focused on autonomous-vehicle simulation, so SynChrono currently requires Chrono::Vehicle; this is not fundamental and adds no extra build dependencies. Visualization goes through Chrono::Irrlicht or Chrono::Sensor.

nodes.label: Deformable Terrain Synchronization
nodes.rationale: Lets multiple vehicles drive off-road and interact with the ruts and deformation each other leaves behind.

nodes.label: SCM deformed-node state message
nodes.rationale: SCM keeps only deformed nodes in a hash map, displaces them only vertically, and carries no soil history, so a list of (int x, int y, double z) fully captures the shared state.

nodes.label: SynSCMTerrainAgent
nodes.rationale: The terrain resets its deformed-node list every physics step but SynChrono only sends every heartbeat, so the agent merges per-step lists into its own map and clears it once per heartbeat.

nodes.label: Terrain synchronization caveats
nodes.rationale: Nothing stops ranks from configuring different soil properties, and if two vehicles modify the same node in one heartbeat the winning update is arbitrary - acceptable because only nodes under the wheels are touched and vehicles are already assumed not to collide.

nodes.label: SynWheeledVehicleAgent
nodes.rationale: A thin wrapper around a ChWheeledVehicle pointer; description carries chassis, wheel and tire visual files plus wheel count so configurations beyond four wheels work, and state carries chassis plus per-wheel poses (tires share wheel poses).

nodes.label: SynTrackedVehicleAgent
nodes.rationale: Wraps a ChTrackedVehicle pointer; left and right meshes are sent separately for sprockets, idlers and road wheels since sides may differ, and counts are sent so arbitrary running-gear configurations reconstruct.

nodes.label: Space-coherent but not space-interactive
nodes.rationale: Only position and orientation are shared, never contact forces, so agents know about each other but cannot physically interact - the deliberate consequence of the weak-coupling assumption.

nodes.label: Track assembly
nodes.rationale: Provides algorithmic auto-assembly of track shoes around sprocket, idler, road wheels and rollers to remove the burden of consistent shoe initialization; specialized routines exist per sprocket-profile / shoe-model combination.

nodes.label: Track assembly templates (SinglePin, DoublePin, BandBushing, BandANCF)
nodes.rationale: The assembly templates differ only in the track-shoe type they carry.

nodes.label: Tracked suspension models
nodes.rationale: Torsion-spring templates with linear or rotational dampers plus a hydropneumatic template; spring and damper forces may be linear, nonlinear, table-lookup or user C++ functors, mirroring the wheeled-vehicle approach.

nodes.label: Road-wheel templates (Double / Single track wheel)
nodes.rationale: The road wheel inside a suspension is templatized on whether the track shoe uses central or lateral guiding pins.

nodes.label: Tracked vehicles
nodes.rationale: A single topology is supported: chassis, driveline, steering mechanism and two track assemblies, each assembly holding sprocket, idler tensioner and arbitrary numbers of suspensions and track shoes.

nodes.label: ChDriver
nodes.rationale: Deliberately minimal base: normalized throttle [0,1], steering [-1,1] and braking [0,1], plus Synchronize to receive vehicle state and Advance for internal dynamics. Derived templates may add gear selection or cross-drive.

nodes.label: ChInteractiveDriver
nodes.rationale: Throttle and braking are coupled so acceleration first zeroes braking; supports lock/unlock of inputs and record/playback via an embedded data driver. Controller handling is tied to Irrlicht, inheriting its button-count limits.

nodes.label: controller.json axis and button mapping
nodes.rationale: Real rigs spread pedals, wheel, H-shifter, sequential shifter, handbrake and button box across several USB devices, so each control names its device plus axis/button and a raw-to-scaled calibration range.

nodes.label: ChDataDriver
nodes.rationale: Open-loop, no feedback: a four-column ASCII file of time, steering, throttle, braking is piecewise-linearly interpolated and held constant past the last entry - suited to standardized test maneuvers and design-of-experiment runs.

nodes.label: PID path-follower controller
nodes.rationale: Pure P leaves residual lateral deviation and oscillates if the gain is too high; I-gain at 5-10% of P removes the residual but must be reset about every two minutes to avoid instability, and D-gain damps oscillation.

nodes.label: Sentinel point and look-ahead distance
nodes.rationale: Models a human driver's anticipation: error is the deviation between a sentinel point ahead of the vehicle and its projection (target point) onto the Bezier path.

nodes.label: ChPathFollowerDriver
nodes.rationale: PID lateral plus PID speed control; works well in extreme maneuvers such as a double lane change.

nodes.label: ChPathFollowerDriverSR
nodes.rationale: Alternative for standard road driving: lateral strategy accounts for human and vehicle properties and anticipates by look-ahead time, so effective look-ahead distance scales with speed.

nodes.label: ChHumanDriver
nodes.rationale: Optimal-speed controller for long curved roads: both lateral and speed control use human behavior, vehicle properties, anticipation and driver field of view; lateral law is shared with ChPathFollowerDriverSR.

nodes.label: HMMWV model
nodes.rationale: M966 troop carrier: double wishbone on both axles, all wheels driven, three-gear automatic with torque converter, Pitman-arm steering; accepts every Chrono tire model.

nodes.label: FEDA model
nodes.rationale: FED ALPHA concept vehicle, 4WD, double wishbone front and rear with anti-roll bar and Pitman-arm steering; only Pacejka 2002 and rigid tires implemented.

nodes.label: Citybus model
nodes.rationale: Leaf-sprung solid axles are modeled functionally, so no leaf blades appear; demonstrates toebar (rotary arm) steering and double wheels.

nodes.label: FMTV (LMTV / MTV) models
nodes.rationale: Both variants model torsional compliance between cabin and cargo; the 6x4 MTV adds a balancer-beam rear bogie.

nodes.label: MAN Kat 1 truck family (5t / 7t / 10t)
nodes.rationale: Coil-sprung link-guided solid axles give very high wheel travel; the box-shaped frame has almost no torsion in the real truck, which justifies the rigid-chassis modeling choice.

nodes.label: UAZ 452 and UAZ 469 models
nodes.rationale: The 469 shares axle and engine components with the 452, differing mainly in steering configuration.

nodes.label: Gator model
nodes.rationale: John Deere electric utility vehicle instrumented for autonomous driving - single wishbone front, rigid rear axle, rear-only brakes, electric motor through a differential.

nodes.label: Generic wheeled vehicle sandbox
nodes.rationale: A testbed for templates and settings; its concrete subsystems are not necessarily mutually consistent because it represents no real vehicle.

nodes.label: M113 tracked model
nodes.rationale: Ten road wheels, two sprockets, two idlers; configurable single- or double-pin track (rubber band track in development), track tension set through the idler tensioning suspension, bogie/torsion-bar road wheels.

nodes.label: Marder tracked model
nodes.rationale: Built only from public data and literature; although the real vehicle uses double-pin tracks the Chrono model currently implements a single-pin track.

nodes.label: Overview of vehicle modeling and simulation
Template-based subsystem design
nodes.rationale: A template fixes bodies, joints, force elements, topology and design parameters for a subsystem type; a concrete vehicle is an instantiation with hardpoints and inertias. This buys modularity without re-deriving each vehicle.

nodes.label: JSON vehicle specification hierarchy
nodes.rationale: As a middleware library Chrono::Vehicle normally needs user-written C++ classes per concrete template, which demands programming experience; nested JSON files provide the same instantiation without code.

nodes.label: ISO vehicle reference frame
nodes.rationale: Chrono::Vehicle models exclusively in a right-handed ISO 8855:2011 frame (X forward, Z up, Y left); each subsystem's hardpoints are given in its own frame and placed relative to the chassis-aligned vehicle frame.

nodes.label: ChWorldFrame
nodes.rationale: Lets a vehicle be simulated in a scene authored in a non-ISO frame (e.g. Y-up) by storing the rotation from ISO to world; it must be set before any other Chrono::Vehicle call.

nodes.label: Synchronize / Advance simulation loop
nodes.rationale: A force-displacement co-simulation scheme where every system exposes Synchronize (data exchange) and Advance (own dynamics). Adopted for modularity, third-party auxiliary models, and co-simulation with external tools - though an all-Chrono setup still solves monolithically.

nodes.label: Thin interface classes for third-party powertrains
ChTerrain base class
nodes.rationale: Height, normal and friction queries only matter for semi-empirical tire models; deformable terrains bypass them and interact through the Chrono collision/contact system with rigid or FEA tires and tracked vehicles.

nodes.label: ChTerrain::FrictionFunctor
nodes.rationale: User-derived functor returning a position-dependent friction coefficient; it only reaches tire models that explicitly consume friction, not general contact.

nodes.label: FlatTerrain
nodes.rationale: An infinite horizontal plane with no collision or contact information, so it works only with semi-empirical tire models.

nodes.label: RigidTerrain
nodes.rationale: A collection of box, OBJ-mesh or BMP-heightmap patches. GetHeight/GetNormal use relatively expensive vertical ray casting; large box patches should be tiled because one huge collision shape degrades collision detection, and mesh patches benefit from a small sweeping-sphere thickness.

nodes.label: Per-contact terrain friction override cost
nodes.rationale: Applying location-dependent friction to real contacts means traversing every contact in the Chrono system once per step to find terrain-patch contacts and rewrite composite material properties - expensive by construction.

nodes.label: CRGTerrain
nodes.rationale: Procedural road built from an OpenCRG specification (requires the OpenCRG SDK at CMake time); carries no collision information so it is limited to semi-empirical tires, but can export the road mesh and Bezier center line.

nodes.label: SCMTerrain (Soil Contact Model)
nodes.rationale: An implicit Cartesian grid deformed by vertical node deflection. The grid is never built explicitly - only deformed nodes live in a hash map - and ray casting, the costliest step, is multithreaded and can be confined to a moving patch. Lightweight enough for near real-time vehicle-terrain forces.

nodes.label: Bekker-Wong pressure-sinkage formulation
nodes.rationale: SCM generalizes Bekker's sigma = (k_c/b + k_phi) y^n to arbitrary 3D contact shapes. Since b (the short side of a rectangular footprint) is undefined for a generic patch, connected patches are found by flooding and b is approximated as 2A/L. Few parameters means easy calibration against experiment.

nodes.label: SCMTerrain::SoilParametersCallback
nodes.rationale: Custom callback returning all soil parameters at an (x,y) point in the terrain reference plane, enabling spatially varying soil.

nodes.label: GranularTerrain
nodes.rationale: DEM patch of monodisperse spheres. Because large-scale granular dynamics is very expensive it supports a moving bin that follows a body (x direction only); fixed boundary particles inhibit bed sliding but conflict with the moving patch.

nodes.label: FEATerrain
nodes.rationale: Deformable terrain from ChElementHexaANCF_3813_9 brick elements with plasticity parameters (yield stress, hardening slope, dilatancy and friction angles).

nodes.label: CRMTerrain (SPH continuous representation)
nodes.rationale: Solves soil-dynamics PDEs with the Chrono::FSI-SPH module; presented as an attractive alternative to granular DEM because it reaches similar accuracy and fidelity at much better computational performance.

nodes.label: A Physics-Based Continuum Model for Versatile, Scalable, and Fast Terramechanics Simulation (arXiv 2507.05643)
Reported CRM speedups (up to 15.9x tracked-vehicle benchmark)
SCM GPU backends
nodes.rationale: Two optional HIP backends move the per-node-independent stages of an SCM step (ray casting and the dense Bekker/Mohr-Coulomb/Janosi force loop) onto the GPU; contact-patch clustering and bulldozing stay on the CPU because they are not per-node independent.

nodes.label: GPU eligibility checks and CPU fallback
nodes.rationale: Force GPU needs uniform soil (no RegisterSoilParametersCallback), rigid ChBody contactables and at least min_hits (8192) hits; ray-cast GPU needs registered active domains with triangle-mesh collision shapes, the only type the kernels intersect. Primitive or convex-hull models stay on the CPU path and report once on stderr instead of silently returning no hits.

nodes.label: scm_gpu::Config settings
nodes.rationale: enabled, min_hits (8192), reserve_hits (65536), async HIP streams for pack/compute/scatter, and profile timings to stderr.

nodes.label: FP32 kernels for cross-vendor determinism
nodes.rationale: Ray-cast kernels run FP32 on every platform so a model traces the same trajectory on AMD and NVIDIA rather than diverging by vendor; FP64 is reachable via SCM_RAYCAST_GPU_PRECISION for validation only.

nodes.label: HIP on NVIDIA default
nodes.rationale: The kernels exist only in HIP and compile through HIP's NVIDIA platform with nvcc, so 'is HIP available' and 'can this use the GPU' are the same question - hence CHRONO_ENABLE_HIP_ON_NVIDIA defaults ON, while Chrono::DEM and FSI::SPH still resolve to CUDA on NVIDIA.

nodes.label: Systematic sinkage offset vs the Bullet CPU path
nodes.rationale: On demo_ROBOT_Viper_SCM the wheel sinks ~5.5 cm on the GPU ray-cast backend versus ~4.3 cm through Bullet, consistently across resolutions and vendors. EnableRaycastGpuReference (same algorithm on CPU) agrees within 0.09%, so the gap is formulation, not hardware: ~2% from the force backend, millimeters from collision margin, micrometers from kernel precision.

nodes.label: Vehicle visualization
nodes.rationale: Chrono::VSG is the recommended run-time system, especially for CRM deformable terrain which the Irrlicht-based system does not support.

nodes.label: VSG vehicle visualization plugin
nodes.rationale: Adds vehicle-specific capabilities on top of base Chrono::VSG: chase camera, vehicle telemetry display, per-subsystem visibility control.

nodes.label: ChWheeledVehicleVisualSystemIrrlicht / ChTrackedVehicleVisualSystemIrrlicht
nodes.rationale: Extend ChVisualSystemIrrlicht with a vehicle-centric camera, vehicle statistics (speed, driver inputs, powertrain and sprocket torques) and contact-force rendering for tracked vehicles.

nodes.label: POV-Ray off-line rendering workflow
nodes.rationale: WriteVisualizationAssets dumps per-frame CSV of body poses, visual assets and selected joints; meshes become POV-Ray macros named after the mesh; renderZ.pov batch-processes frames and converts the Z-up right-handed ISO data into POV-Ray's Y-up left-handed frame. The same dump also drives other engines such as Mitsuba.

nodes.label: ChSuspensionTestRig
nodes.rationale: Tests a whole suspension assembly specified standalone from JSON, as an axle in a vehicle JSON file, or as an axle of an already-initialized vehicle. The Platform variant actuates through the tires with two rigid platforms; the Pushrod variant drives the spindles directly.

nodes.label: ChTireTestRig
nodes.rationale: Single-tire rig over rigid, SCM or granular terrain; varies longitudinal speed, wheel angular speed and slip angle over time, can auto-select speeds to enforce a target longitudinal slip, and holds camber fixed. Any tire model works but only with a compatible terrain model.

nodes.label: ChSteering (steering mechanism base class)
nodes.rationale: Base class contract: every derived steering template must expose a steering link body so that a steerable suspension can attach through its tierods; all hardpoints are given in a mechanism reference frame the template is free to choose.

nodes.label: Pitman Arm Steering Template
nodes.rationale: Modeled as a four-bar linkage: Pitman arm joined to the steering link by a universal joint and to the chassis by a revolute joint driven by the steering input; the idler arm is modeled as a composite revolute-spherical joint to avoid redundant constraints.

nodes.label: Rack-Pinion Steering Template
nodes.rationale: Purely kinematic model: rather than modeling gear teeth, the rack displacement is computed from pinion radius, max pinion angle and normalized steering input, then imposed on a prismatic joint.

nodes.label: Rack Displacement Equation d = r(alpha_max * s)
Rotary Arm Steering Template
nodes.rationale: A simple lever arm rotating about an axis; chosen for trucks, farm tractors and combine harvesters where it pairs with solid bellcrank and solid toebar axles.

nodes.label: Multiple Steering Mechanisms per Vehicle
nodes.rationale: A wheeled vehicle may carry several steering mechanisms (one per steerable axle) and conversely one mechanism may drive several steerable axles.

nodes.label: ChSuspension (suspension base class)
nodes.rationale: Base class contract: a suspension template must supply left/right wheel spindles on revolute joints plus two ChShaft spindle axles so a driveline can be attached; the suspension reference frame may be relocated but not reoriented, staying parallel to the chassis ISO frame.

nodes.label: Left-Side Hardpoint Mirroring
nodes.rationale: Hardpoints are authored only for the left side and mirrored to build the right side, halving the specification data and guaranteeing symmetry by construction.

nodes.label: ChDoubleWishboneReduced (simplified double wishbone)
nodes.rationale: Control arms are replaced by two distance constraints each; valid when control-arm mass and inertia are negligible relative to the other bodies, trading fidelity for fewer bodies.

nodes.label: ChMacPhersonStrut
nodes.rationale: Preferred for small to mid-sized front-wheel-drive passenger cars with transverse engine/gearbox.

nodes.label: ChMultiLink
nodes.rationale: Similar to a double wishbone axle but the trailing arm can carry high longitudinal forces.

nodes.label: ChSolidThreeLinkAxle
nodes.rationale: Allows very high wheel travel that leaf springs cannot deliver; air/coil springs require a link-guided axle, hence the three-link guidance.

nodes.label: ChLeafspringAxle
nodes.rationale: Work-alike model: the complex guiding behavior of leaf springs is replaced by a special joint at the center of the axle tube plus coil springs, which reproduces rolling behavior close to a real leaf-spring axle at much lower cost.

nodes.label: ChSAELeafspringAxle
nodes.rationale: Follows the SAE Spring Design Handbook so that axle motion under wheel travel and the tie-up effect from longitudinal forces are reproduced correctly, unlike the work-alike leaf-spring model.

nodes.label: SAE Leaf Spring Kinematic Model (5 points, 6 bodies)
nodes.rationale: Leaf-spring kinematics defined by 5 points and realized as 6 rigid bodies (front leaf, front clamp, rear clamp, rear leaf, shackle) joined by rotational springs whose stiffness the user tunes.

nodes.label: ChRigidPinnedAxle
nodes.rationale: Unsprung axle that can swing about a pivot against the chassis, used when an unsprung system must run on undulated terrain without wheel lift-off.

nodes.label: ChGenericWheeledSuspension
nodes.rationale: Escape hatch for arbitrary topology: the user declares bodies, joints, distance constraints and TSDAs, flags components as mirrored, and the right-side counterparts are generated automatically.

nodes.label: Rigid Tire Model Class
nodes.rationale: Simplest class: the tire is fully rigid and interacts through the same friction/contact algorithms as any rigid body. Useful for debugging, for runtime-critical runs, and whenever the terrain is much softer than the tire.

nodes.label: Handling (Semi-Empirical) Tire Model Class
nodes.rationale: Designed for flat road surfaces with single- or four-point contact; not suitable for off-road simulation on deformable terrain, where only rigid or FEA tires apply.

nodes.label: FEA-Based Tire Model Class
nodes.rationale: Most accurate but most expensive class; uniquely able to represent flexibility of tire and ground simultaneously, which matters for off-road mobility studies.

nodes.label: ChPac02Tire (Pacejka 2002)
nodes.rationale: Extends the earlier Magic Formula with contact-patch slip state equations so that transient (non steady-state slip) maneuvers are accurate; inflation-pressure and large-camber terms were left out for lack of reference data.

nodes.label: ChTMeasyTire (Tire Model Made Easy)
nodes.rationale: Chosen for ease of parameterization: a full parameter set can be estimated from few inputs using known truck/car sets. The Chrono port omits belt dynamics and dynamic parking torque of the commercial version.

nodes.label: ChFialaTire
nodes.rationale: Brush-model based with few coefficients and slip state equations for good behavior at low/zero forward speed, but it assumes zero camber and generates no overturning moment, so it should not be used for serious handling work.

nodes.label: Envelope Contact Algorithm (Sui & Hershey)
nodes.rationale: Added so handling tire models can be used for ride tests on undulated roads and obstacle crossing, which single-point contact cannot represent, while keeping numerical effort low.

nodes.label: Steady State Cornering (SSC) Validation Test
nodes.rationale: Vehicle circles starting at the Ackermann speed with speed raised in steps until maximum lateral acceleration or engine power is exhausted; run in both left and right turns to expose vehicle asymmetry.

nodes.label: Understeer vs Oversteer Safety Criterion
nodes.rationale: A road vehicle for average drivers should understeer: oversteering vehicles turn toward the circle origin and go unstable because the rear wheels run out of lateral slip reserve.

nodes.label: Road Vehicle Dynamics - Fundamentals and Modeling with MATLAB (Rill & Castro, CRC Press 2020)
irrlicht::ChVisualSystemIrrlicht
nodes.rationale: Longest-serving Chrono real-time renderer, so it carries the widest feature set: problem size / timing readouts, link frame and force rendering, contact reaction display, all surfaced through an info panel.

nodes.label: Run-Time Visualization Systems
nodes.rationale: Optimized for fast real-time rendering with user interfaces and live simulation information.

nodes.label: Offline / Postprocess Visualization Systems
nodes.rationale: Used for higher-quality renderings that cannot meet run-time constraints.

nodes.label: Renderer-Agnostic Visualization Abstraction
nodes.rationale: Bodies, meshes, particles and even physics-free shapes are described independently of any renderer so Chrono stays unbound to a single engine and new rendering systems can be added easily.

nodes.label: Tutorial: Load a STEP File and Simulate a Robot (demo_CAS_robot.cpp)
nodes.rationale: Marked obsolete in the docs and in need of deep updating to the latest Chrono version.

nodes.label: ChCascadeDoc::GetNamedShape path lookup
nodes.rationale: Addresses sub-assemblies like a Unix path with wildcards, and disambiguates repeated shape names with a #N instance suffix.

nodes.label: Auxiliary Marker Placeholder Convention
nodes.rationale: Dummy 'marker' parts are inserted in the CAD assembly aligned with each joint axis, so the C++ side can recover joint positions and orientations from the STEP file instead of hard-coding coordinates.

nodes.label: SolidEdge Assembly Renaming Issue
nodes.rationale: SolidEdge rewrites user assembly names to Assem1, Assem2, ... on STEP export, so the recommended workaround is to Dump the hierarchy and map the generated names back to the intended part names.

nodes.label: Teaching-Mode Inverse Kinematics via Lock Constraint
nodes.rationale: Locking the hand marker to a driven marker yields inverse kinematics for any robot, including parallel manipulators and complex chains, without deriving an analytic IK expression.

nodes.label: MINRES Solver Choice for Kinematic Chains
nodes.rationale: Fixed-point solvers (SOR, SSOR) converge poorly here because the hand at the end of the chain is far lighter than the other bodies; MINRES is fast and precise enough to keep the joints assembled, though unsuited to frictional collisions.

nodes.label: Root Frame Transformation for CAD Axis Convention
nodes.rationale: Most CADs treat Y as horizontal while the simulation wants Y vertical, so a single root frame quaternion product pre-transforms every imported body.

nodes.label: Two-Way Co-Simulation Pattern
nodes.rationale: The system state is partitioned between the two solvers, which advance independently and synchronize periodically; tightly coupled subsystems force frequent synchronization.

nodes.label: TCP/IP Socket Variable Exchange
nodes.rationale: Chrono acts as server and Simulink as client; the Chrono state is interpolated linearly over the Simulink sub-steps while the Simulink state is held as a Zero Order Hold on the Chrono side.

nodes.label: Simulink CoSimulate Block
nodes.rationale: Only one CoSimulate block may exist per model; larger interfaces are handled by widening the input and output vectors with Mux/De-Mux rather than adding blocks.

nodes.label: Communication Step Size Selection
nodes.rationale: Hydraulic systems are stiff, so the exchange interval must be very small; larger steps make the latency of the extrapolated coupling variables produce numerical instability, while small steps slow the co-simulation down.

nodes.label: Where to Split a System for Co-Simulation
nodes.rationale: Split at an interface where the connecting variables carry low frequencies: the higher the frequency crossing the interface, the smaller the communication step must be.

nodes.label: Dead Linear Actuator (ChLinkTSDA with zero stiffness/damping)
nodes.rationale: A zero-stiffness, zero-damping TSDA is used purely as the carrier for the externally supplied hydraulic force between two bodies.

nodes.label: Chrono::DEM Module
nodes.rationale: GPU-accelerated granular dynamics through the penalty-based discrete element method (SMC).

nodes.label: demo_DEM_ballCosim
nodes.rationale: Co-simulation example: the mesh sphere's dynamics are advanced by ChSystem while the contact forces come from the Chrono::DEM granular system.

nodes.label: Doxygen Documentation Build Workflow
nodes.rationale: Docs live in the chrono/doxygen folder and are built by running doxygen there; output defaults to /tmp/chrono_doxygen and is retargeted via OUTPUT_DIRECTORY in Doxyfile.

nodes.label: MediaWiki to Markdown Migration Conventions
nodes.rationale: The guide pairs each old MediaWiki construct with its Markdown replacement (links, headings, Details blocks becoming div class=well) so legacy wiki pages can be ported mechanically.

nodes.label: Chrono White Paper
nodes.rationale: Technical/analytical document anchoring a software implementation in Chrono; kept uniform by writing every one against a shared LaTeX class.

nodes.label: urlChronoAPIclass / urlChronoAPInamespace / urlChronoAPImodule Macros
nodes.rationale: Turn a namespaced C++ name into the decorated .html page name of the Doxygen-generated Chrono API docs.

nodes.label: Manual White Paper LaTeX Build
nodes.rationale: Compiling white paper LaTeX sources is deliberately outside the automatic Doxygen toolchain, so authors must build, check cross links and upload by hand.

nodes.label: demo_FMI_craneFMU
nodes.rationale: Wraps an inverted-pendulum crane mast plus payload; takes an external actuation force as its continuous input and publishes actuator length and length rate as outputs.

nodes.label: demo_FMI_actuatorFMU
nodes.rationale: Wraps a hydraulic actuator (piston, directional valve, hoses, pump, oil tank); consumes actuator length and rate and publishes actuator force.

nodes.label: FMU_WheeledVehicle
nodes.rationale: Four-wheel vehicle with powertrain and transmission but no tires, specified entirely through JSON; must be co-simulated with a driver FMU and four tire systems.

nodes.label: FMU_ForceElementTire
nodes.rationale: Wraps a ChForceElementTire handling tire defined by JSON; needs a wheel state from the vehicle and terrain height, normal and friction at a single query point.

nodes.label: FMU_PathFollowerDriver
nodes.rationale: Lateral path-following PID plus longitudinal PID cruise controller; the path comes from a data file and the FMU emits steering, throttle and braking commands.

nodes.label: CRM Continuum Representation of Granular Material
demo_FSI-SPH_Cratering
nodes.rationale: Falling sphere into a granular bed, kept as a validation case against published experimental and analytical results.

nodes.label: Chrono IRRLICHT Module Tutorials
nodes.rationale: Irrlicht is treated as the default run-time visualization system, so its installation is covered by the main Chrono install guide rather than repeated here.

nodes.label: Irrlicht Run-Time Visualization Module
nodes.rationale: Required run-time dependency of the MBS starter demos; it supplies both the 3D view and the GUI/keyboard event plumbing used for interactive demos, which is why nearly every introductory demo is written against it.

nodes.label: VSG Run-Time Visualization Module
nodes.rationale: Optional alternative run-time visualizer offered by a subset of demos (bricks, friction), letting the same simulation code be rendered by either backend.

nodes.label: Contact Surface Material
nodes.rationale: Contact properties are carried by a surface-material object attached to bodies rather than by the bodies themselves, so friction/restitution can be shared or varied per contact zone.

nodes.label: Stepper Settings Precision/Speed Trade-off
nodes.rationale: The demo exists partly to show how stepper settings are tuned toward either higher precision or higher computing speed.

nodes.label: Conveyor Belt Primitive
nodes.rationale: A dedicated body type whose surface imposes a tangential velocity at contact, so a belt can be simulated without modelling a chain of discrete belt segments.

nodes.label: Real-Time Integration Step Adaptation
nodes.rationale: Chrono adapts the integration step to the speed of the CPU so a real-time application keeps wall-clock pace with simulated time, trading per-step accuracy for interactive responsiveness.

nodes.label: Skeleton Line Rendering of Joints
nodes.rationale: The simplest possible Chrono/Irrlicht integration: joint coordinates are used directly as end-points of polygonal lines redrawn each frame, avoiding any visual asset system so the coupling between physics state and rendering stays obvious to a beginner.

nodes.label: OBJ Mesh Loading for Visualization
nodes.rationale: Visual .OBJ meshes are loaded independently of collision geometry, so a detailed appearance can be paired with simpler collision shapes.

nodes.label: Direct Solver vs Iterative Solver
nodes.rationale: A direct solver is selected instead of the default iterative solver to obtain the highest precision on a small, well-conditioned linkage, where the cost of a direct factorization is affordable.

nodes.label: Rolling and Spinning (Drilling) Friction
nodes.rationale: Optional friction terms that matter for rolling objects such as wheels and spheres, left off by default because of their cost.

nodes.label: ChLinkLockGear
nodes.rationale: Simplified kinematic constraint representing gear interaction in 3D space; chosen specifically to avoid simulating contacts between gear teeth, which would be prohibitively expensive and stiff.

nodes.label: ChLinkLockPulley
nodes.rationale: Simplified pulley constraint in 3D space, the belt-drive counterpart of the gear constraint, again replacing contact simulation with an algebraic transmission relation.

nodes.label: ChCoordsys and ChFrame Reference Management
nodes.rationale: Coordinate-system and frame objects used to compose rotations of references; the gear and mecanum demos both lean on them because assembling transmissions and omnidirectional wheels is mostly a problem of nested frame transforms.

nodes.label: Barrel Collision Shape
nodes.rationale: Primitive used to model the angled rollers of a mecanum wheel; a dedicated analytic shape avoids meshing each roller while preserving the rolling contact behaviour that produces omnidirectional motion.

nodes.label: Real-Time Keyboard Interaction in Irrlicht View
Chrono Motors (Rotational and Linear)
nodes.rationale: Motors are catalogued as variants A.1-A.5 (rotational) and B.1-B.6 (linear), i.e. a family of actuation abstractions differing by what is prescribed (angle, speed, torque) rather than a single configurable class.

nodes.label: Force Accumulators (custom applied forces)
nodes.rationale: Used here to inject a simplified aerodynamic drag without writing a dedicated force element.

nodes.label: ChLinkDistance
nodes.rationale: Used to represent massless rods, saving computational effort: a single distance constraint replaces an extra body plus two joints in the double-wishbone linkage.

nodes.label: ChLinkSpring
nodes.rationale: Spring-damper element used for the suspension compliance, applied as a force element between two bodies rather than as a constraint.

nodes.label: Zone-Dependent Friction Coefficient
